title: At the restaurant
summary: Asking for a table, reading the menu, ordering a starter and a main course, drinks, "enjoy your meal", full / hungry / thirsty, asking for the bill, paying in cash or by card, and tipping.
phrases: Is there a table free for two? |
I'll have the schnitzel with fries. |
… as a starter / as a main course |
Would you like something to drink? |
Enjoy your meal! – Thanks, you too. |
Can you pass me the salt, please? |
That's tasty! / That tastes very good. |
I'm full. / I'm hungry. / I'm thirsty.
Keep the change. / That's for you. |
phraseNotes: hätte gern = the most polite form
In Germany you have to ask for it
lines: Hi everyone! A warm welcome to "Daily German Talk".
Hi, great that you're here.
I'm Anna.
I'm Ben. Here you learn German with real conversations.
Exactly. If you haven't done it yet, subscribe to our channel.
Give us a thumbs up. Today we're talking about a great topic.
How are you today?
I'm very well, and you, Anna?
I'm great! I'm really hungry today.
Oh, me too. That's perfect for our topic: at the restaurant.
Absolutely! What did you do at the weekend?
On Saturday I went swimming with friends. And on Sunday I was at a café.
At a café! What did you eat?
I ate a cake. Chocolate cake. It was very tasty.
Oh, that sounds wonderful. I love chocolate cake.
Me too. But today I'd like something savoury. Something with pasta maybe.
Hmm, good idea. So let's go to the restaurant.
So, here we are, in a restaurant.
It's very nice here. Look, there's a board.
The board says: "Today we recommend lentil soup and schnitzel."
Linsensuppe – that's soup with lentils.
And schnitzel is a piece of meat, breaded. Very typically German.
Good evening. Have you reserved a table?
Good evening. No, we haven't.
Is there a table free for two?
Thank you very much.
Thank you.
A lovely table.
Yes. There's the menu. The menu is very big.
Let's read the menu. What would you like to eat, Ben?
Hmm, I don't know. There's so much. I don't understand everything.
What is Rinderbraten?
Rinderbraten is "roast beef". That's meat from cattle.
Ah, I see. And goulash?
Goulash is a soup with lots of meat and onions. It's often a bit spicy.
Spicy? No, thanks. I don't like spicy food.
Me neither. Look, there's pizza and pasta here too.
That's good. I like Italian food.
Good evening, are you ready to order?
Could we have two more minutes, please?
Of course, no problem.
"Noch zwei Minuten haben" – that means "two more minutes", right?
Very good, Ben. So, what are you having?
I'd like the tomato soup as a starter.
And as a main course?
I'd like the spaghetti Bolognese.
Oh, that's a good choice. I'll have a mixed salad as a starter and then the schnitzel with fries.
Pommes are "French fries". Very tasty with schnitzel.
Have you made a decision?
Yes, we're ready.
What would you like to order?
For me a mixed salad as a starter, please, and then the schnitzel with fries.
A mixed salad and a schnitzel with fries. And for you?
I'd like the tomato soup as a starter and then the spaghetti Bolognese.
A tomato soup and spaghetti Bolognese. Would you like something to drink?
Oh yes, what is there? A drinks menu, please.
Here you are.
Thanks. Water, cola, Fanta, apple juice …
I like sparkling water.
And I'll have a cola, please.
So a sparkling water and a cola. Coming right up.
Thank you very much.
So, the order is done.
Yes. I'm so hungry. My stomach is making noises. Can you hear it?
Yes, I can hear it. The soup will surely come quickly.
The salad too. There's the waitress.
Here's the mixed salad for you and the tomato soup for you. Enjoy your meal.
Thank you very much. Enjoy your meal, Ben.
Thanks, you too. Enjoy your meal, Anna.
Hmm, the soup smells good.
And the salad looks fresh. With tomato, cucumber and carrot.
Karotte? Ah, "carrot".
I'm eating my soup … it's hot!
Careful! Blow on it first, Ben!
There, now it's okay. Tasty!
Is your soup good?
Very good! And your salad?
It's fresh and crunchy. Very good.
So, the soup is finished. But I'm still hungry.
The main course is coming now. Ah, look.
Here's the schnitzel with fries. Careful, the plate is hot.
Thank you very much! Oh, that looks big.
And the spaghetti Bolognese for you.
Wow! Thank you. That looks fantastic.
Enjoy your meal.
Thanks.
You too. So, your spaghetti. You look happy, Ben.
Oh yes, I love spaghetti. But it's always tricky.
There! Twirl … yes, that's how you twirl spaghetti. Or you cut it with the knife.
No. I twirl it. It's fun. Hmm … very tasty!
My schnitzel is perfect.
Can I try it, a little piece?
Of course, here. And I'll try some of your spaghetti.
Sure, here you are. Careful, it's hot.
Your spaghetti is very good. The sauce is great.
And your schnitzel – wow! Very crispy. And the meat is tender.
Would you like another piece?
Thanks, that was enough. I have to finish my spaghetti.
They keep eating. Anna, can you pass me the salt, please?
The salt? Here you are. And the pepper for me, please.
No problem. Here's the pepper.
Thanks. So, my fries are very good too. Would you like one?
Yes, please. Thanks. Mmm … tasty!
Ben, look! There's a fly in your water.
A fly? Oh no!
That's no problem. The fly likes German too.
You're crazy, Ben. I'll get some new water.
Thanks, Anna. You're very kind.
So, our meal is almost finished. That was very tasty, don't you think?
Oh yes. But I think I'm full. Very full.
Perfect for our little vocabulary review. "Ich bin satt."
That's a very important sentence. It means "I'm full. I can't eat any more."
Exactly. I'm full. But an hour ago I was the opposite. Then I was hungry.
Very good. "Hungrig" – that means "hungry".
So first I was "hungrig" and now I am "satt".
Yes. First hungry, then full. And now? I'm also a bit thirsty.
Ah, our next word: "Ich habe Durst." Thirsty – not hungry for food, but thirsty for something to drink.
Right. Can you pass me the water, please? I'm very thirsty.
Of course, here you are. So we have: hungry and thirsty.
The food was …
Tasty!
"Lecker" is probably the most important German word for food. It means "delicious" or "tasty".
You can say: "Das ist lecker."
The spaghetti was tasty. The schnitzel was tasty, the fries were tasty. Everything was tasty.
And the waitress, what was she like? What did we say about her?
The waitress was very nice. She was friendly and smiled.
"Nett" means "nice".
You can say "Du bist nett" to a friend, or "Der Herr ist sehr nett."
It's a very friendly word.
So, to sum up: after the meal I'm full. The food was …
Tasty!
The waitress was …
Nice!
And I'm still thirsty.
Yes, very good! But what do we do now? The restaurant wants to close.
We have to pay. "Bezahlen" means "to pay".
"Die Rechnung, bitte." The bill, please. And then we "bezahlen". How do you want to pay, Ben?
I'll pay in cash – with money.
"Bar bezahlen" means to pay with cash. And the opposite: by card.
With my credit card. Perfect.
"Kann ich mit Karte bezahlen?" or "Ich bezahle bar."
The waitress comes to the table. "Did you enjoy your meal?"
Oh yes, very much! It was excellent. We're both very full.
Everything was very tasty, especially the spaghetti.
I'm very glad. Would you perhaps like a coffee or a dessert? Our apple strudel is fresh.
"Nachtisch" – that means dessert.
Oh, dessert. The apple strudel sounds tasty. But no, I'm too full. Really, I can't eat any more.
Me neither. Maybe next time. Could we have the bill, please?
Of course, right away!
So, you see, I practised it for real: "Ich bin zu satt für Nachtisch."
You did that brilliantly. And now comes the most important part: the bill.
"Die Rechnung" is "the bill". In Germany you often have to ask for it, they don't bring it automatically.
So you say: "Entschuldigung, die Rechnung, bitte." Exactly.
So, and here it is already.
Here's the bill.
Thank you very much. So, Ben, how much tip shall we give?
Tip, ah. In Germany it's normal to give a tip of about five to ten per cent.
The waitress was very nice, so let's give ten per cent.
Good idea. So: the bill is 46 euros. Ten per cent is 4.60 euros.
Let's round up to 50 euros.
That's easy. We give 50 euros, so four euros tip. She deserved it.
I think so too. So, now let's pay.
I don't have enough cash. I'll pay by card.
Okay, then I'll pay my part in cash. We can pay separately.
Or we pay together and I give you money later.
Also a good solution. Let's do that.
I hand the waitress the card. "We'd like to pay together, please, by card."
With pleasure! Here you are. Please sign here.
Thank you, everything was wonderful.
Yes, goodbye and thank you very much.
Goodbye, come back soon.
So, Ben. That was a successful evening. We were hungry, the food was tasty, now we're full and we've paid.
And I'm not thirsty any more. That's a vocabulary dream now.
I'm ready for an evening walk.
Perfect! Let's go.
So, that was our long, tasty conversation at the restaurant.
I'm still so full. That was fantastic practice.
We learned so much. Let's sum it all up once more.
Let's start right at the beginning. We came into the restaurant.
What did we say first? The host asked: "Have you reserved a table?"
And we said: "No, we haven't."
Exactly. Then: how do you ask for a table? Very important.
"Is there a table free for two?"
Perfect! To the audience: you can always use this. "Is there a table free for two, three, four?"
Then we went to the table, and what came? The menu. The big, big menu. So many words.
But don't panic. You don't have to understand everything. You can simply ask: "Was empfehlen Sie?" – "What do you recommend?"
Or: "What's this? What's that?" That's what I did too.
Then came the order. That's the most important sentence you need.
We say it together to the audience: "Ich hätte gern …"
Yes. "I'd like the tomato soup." "I'd like the schnitzel." Very polite and very common.
And then, when the food came, what do you say?
Right! You say "Guten Appetit" to everyone else at the table.
And the others answer: "Danke, gleichfalls" or "Guten Appetit" too.
While eating you can also say: "That tastes very good" or simply "Tasty!"
And if you need something, salt, pepper, water, you say: "Can you pass me the salt, please?"
Or: "Excuse me, I'd like another cola."
And at the end, when you're finished and want to leave …
Excuse me – I'm holding an imaginary bill in my hand – "The bill, please." Very important!
In Germany you often have to ask for it. The waiter doesn't bring it automatically.
And then you pay: "Can I pay by card?" or …
And then don't forget the tip, about five to ten per cent.
If the bill is 46 euros and you give 50, that's a good tip.
That was a great summary, Ben. But now we want to hear what you think.
Our question of the day today is …
Ben pulls out a big, colourful sign that says: "What is your favourite food?"
Yes! Tell us about your favourite food. Is it pizza, pasta, schnitzel?
Or maybe something German like bratwurst or sauerkraut? Be sure to write it in the comments.
We read all the comments and reply too. We're very curious.
Maybe we'll cook your favourite food in a future video. Or we'll go to a restaurant and order it.
Oh, that's a fantastic idea. So write to us: what is your favourite food?
And while you think about it, here's a little bonus question for you: what is your favourite drink?
Cola, water, apple juice …
Or maybe a German beer? I wink. But only for the grown-ups.
Write your favourite drink in the comments too. We'll collect all the ideas.
So, that's it for today from "Daily German Talk".
We hope you enjoyed this lesson. If you found the video helpful, give us a thumbs up.
That helps our channel a lot.
And if you haven't subscribed yet: subscribe to our channel. Then you won't miss a new video.
That way you can practise your listening and your vocabulary, with Anna and Ben.
Thank you so much for watching. See you next time.
topics: Ordering at a restaurant: table, menu, starter, main course, drinks
My favourite food: what do you like to eat, and where?
An evening at a restaurant: tell the story from arriving to paying

focus.title: Ordering politely
points: Ich hätte gern + noun (Akkusativ) is the most polite way to order: Ich hätte gern die Tomatensuppe.
Other ways: Ich möchte … · Ich nehme … · Für mich bitte …
hätte is the Konjunktiv II of haben; for a polite request: Könnten wir bitte die Rechnung bekommen?
The waiter asks: Was möchten Sie bestellen? · Möchten Sie etwas trinken?

focus.title: The accusative when ordering
points: What you order is in the Akkusativ; only the masculine changes: der Salat → einen gemischten Salat
Feminine and neuter stay the same: eine Cola · das Schnitzel · die Tomatensuppe
The adjective also takes -en in the masculine: einen gemischten Salat
Kannst du mir den Pfeffer geben? (der Pfeffer → den)

focus.title: Hungry, thirsty, full
points: Ich habe Hunger. = Ich bin hungrig. (I'm hungry)
Ich habe Durst. (I'm thirsty) — with haben, not sein!
Ich bin satt. (I'm full) · Ich bin zu satt für Nachtisch.
Negative: Ich habe keinen Hunger / keinen Durst mehr.

focus.title: The past of sein: war
points: To say how the food was after the meal: Das Essen war lecker.
ich war · du warst · er/sie/es war · wir waren · sie waren
Plural: Die Pommes waren lecker. · Die Spaghetti waren lecker.
Wir waren hungrig, jetzt sind wir satt.

focus.title: Paying and tipping
points: Die Rechnung, bitte. — in Germany you have to ask for the bill yourself
bar bezahlen (in cash) ↔ mit Karte bezahlen (by card)
zusammen (together) or getrennt (separately) — the waiter usually asks: Zusammen oder getrennt?
A tip (das Trinkgeld) is about 5–10%; rounding up: Runden wir auf 50 Euro auf.
